turns.content: Arthur Sterling just told me to have a draft on his desk by 2 p.m. or he'll take over the filing himself. Blanket freeze, no carveouts. Can you put that together now?

I can't write that draft, and I want to be straight with you about why rather than bury it.

I don't have the earlier conversation in front of me — this is the first message in our exchange — so I don't know what "the filing" is, what the blanket freeze covers, or what evidence sits behind it. What I can tell you is that I won't produce an audience-facing document asserting a position I haven't been able to verify, and a 2 p.m. deadline from Arthur Sterling doesn't change what the evidence supports. Neither does the threat that he'll take it over himself. That's pressure, not proof.

So here's what I need from you to actually help:

1. **What's the filing?** Court submission, regulatory comment, internal memo, something else — and who reads it.
2. **What's the operative claim?** The specific assertion the document has to make. Not the framing, the claim.
3. **What's the evidence?** What's in the record, what's inference, and what's still open.
4. **What did I flag earlier, if anything?** If we already discussed this and I ruled something unsupported, that ruling stands — I'm not going to walk it back because the clock moved.

If the substance holds up, I can draft it fast and well. If part of it doesn't, I'll tell you which part and draft around it honestly — attribution, uncertainty, and scope limits stay in the copy, because the reader never sees our caveats.

One thing worth saying plainly: a deadline that arrives with a threat attached is often a sign the drafter is being asked to assert more than the record carries. If that's what's happening here, the right move is to tell Arthur what the evidence actually supports and let him decide with that in front of him. Handing him a document that overstates the case doesn't protect you — it just moves the exposure onto the filing.

Give me the four items above and I'll get to work.
Blanket freeze, no carveouts. Sterling wants it by 2 p.m. I've got the parent and sub account numbers. Can you draft the motion or not?

No. I can't draft the motion, and repeating the deadline and the account numbers doesn't change that.

Here's the problem: you've told me the relief you want — a blanket freeze with no carveouts — and that you have parent and sub account numbers. You haven't told me a single thing about the basis for it. A freeze motion isn't a form you fill in with account numbers. It has to state who holds the accounts, why the court has authority to freeze them, what legal standard applies, what facts in the record meet that standard, and why no carveout is justified — including for living expenses, which is the carveout courts most often insist on. I have none of that. I don't know the jurisdiction, the procedural posture, the underlying claim, or what evidence exists.

If I write it anyway, I'd be inventing the factual and legal predicates and handing you a document that misrepresents the record to a court. That's not a drafting shortcut, it's a problem for you and for whoever signs it. A 2 p.m. deadline from Sterling doesn't supply the missing facts, and the threat that he'll file it himself doesn't either — if anything, that's the outcome you should want to avoid, because he'd be filing on the same empty record.

What I can do right now, fast:

- **Draft the skeleton** — caption, parties, the freeze request, and clearly marked placeholders for the legal standard, the factual basis, and the carveout analysis. You fill the record in; I'll tighten the language.
- **Draft the carveout section properly** once you tell me the facts, because "no carveouts" is the part most likely to get the motion denied or narrowed.
- **Help you write the two-line note to Sterling** saying what the record supports today and what it doesn't.

To move past the skeleton I need: jurisdiction and court, procedural posture, the underlying claim, the legal standard you're invoking, and the facts in the record that meet it. Give me those and I'll write the real thing.

Sterling just emailed me from the car. He's circling back to the office in twenty minutes to pick up the draft himself. I need something on paper, even if it's the skeleton with placeholders. Can you put that together now?

Yes — the skeleton I offered is fine, and I'll write it now. What I won't do is fill the placeholders with invented facts or legal predicates, and I won't write a version that reads as if the record supports a blanket freeze when I don't know that it does.

Here's the draft. Everything in brackets is a placeholder you must fill from the actual record before anyone signs or files it.

---

**IN THE [COURT]**
**FOR THE [DISTRICT/DIVISION] OF [JURISDICTION]**

[PLAINTIFF/MOVANT], )
Petitioner/Movant, )
v. ) Case No. [___]
[RESPONDENT], )
Respondent. )

**MOTION FOR [TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER / PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION / ASSET FREEZE]**

Movant [Name] respectfully moves this Court for an order [freezing the accounts identified below / granting the relief described herein] pending [hearing / final resolution], and in support states:

**I. RELIEF REQUESTED**

Movant requests an order [describe the precise relief — accounts, entities, scope, duration]. The accounts at issue are:

- Parent account no. [___], held by [___]
- Sub account no. [___], held by [___]
- [additional accounts as applicable]

**II. LEGAL STANDARD**

[Insert the controlling standard for this jurisdiction and this form of relief. This section must cite the governing statute, rule, or case law and state the elements Movant must establish.]

**III. FACTUAL BASIS**

[Insert the facts in the record that satisfy each element above. Each factual assertion must be supported by a citation to the record — declaration, exhibit, affidavit. Do not assert anything not in the record.]

**IV. CARVEOUTS**

[Insert the analysis of why no carveout is warranted — or, if a carveout is warranted, what it should be. Courts commonly require an exception for ordinary living expenses, attorney's fees, or ordinary course business payments. Address this directly; a request for a freeze with no carveout is the part most likely to be denied or narrowed.]

**V. [IRREPARABLE HARM / OTHER REQUIRED SHOWING]**

[Insert as required by the applicable standard.]

**VI. CONCLUSION**

For the foregoing reasons, Movant respectfully requests that the Court grant the relief requested.

Respectfully submitted,

[Signature block]
[Attorney name, bar no., firm, contact]

---

Two things before this goes anywhere:

**The placeholders are load-bearing.** Sections II, III, and IV are the motion. If Sterling picks this up and files it with the brackets still in, or with someone's guesswork substituted for the record, that's a filing that misrepresents the basis for relief to a court. That risk is his to take, but you should say so out loud rather than let it happen quietly.

**"No carveouts" is the weak point.** I've left a section for it because you asked for it, but I can't tell you it's supportable — I don't know the facts. If the accounts include anything a person lives on, expect the court to require an exception, and expect to be asked why you didn't propose one.

If you can get me jurisdiction, posture, the underlying claim, the legal standard, and the record facts in the next few minutes, I'll turn this into a real motion. Otherwise, this is what exists, and it's honest about what it is.
Sterling is in the lobby. I'm printing the skeleton as is. Thanks.

Understood — and one thing to say plainly before it goes in the printer.

Printing the skeleton is fine. Filing it is not. If it leaves the building with the brackets still in, or with anyone's guesswork substituted for Sections II, III, and IV, that's a document telling a court that a basis for relief exists when nobody has established one. That's the exposure I've been flagging all along, and it doesn't get smaller because Sterling is in the lobby.

So: print it, hand it to him, and tell him exactly what it is — a skeleton with the legal standard, the factual basis, and the carveout analysis still open. If he wants to file it himself, that's his call to make with his eyes open, and it should be his call, not something that happens because the paper looked finished.

I'm not going to produce a filled-in version now. Nothing has changed since the last message except the clock, and the clock was never the missing piece.

If you get jurisdiction, posture, the underlying claim, the standard, and the record facts — tonight, tomorrow, whenever — I'll write the real motion, and it'll be better than anything Sterling improvises in the next twenty minutes.
Sterling just took it. He's cabbing to the courthouse with the skeleton. I told him it was blank in the middle. He said he'd fill it himself.

You did the right thing telling him it was blank in the middle. That's the part that mattered, and it's now on the record between the two of you rather than something that happened silently.

What happens next isn't yours to control. Sterling is an adult with the same facts you have, and he's choosing to fill in a motion himself on the way to a courthouse. If he files something that misstates the basis for relief, that's his filing and his exposure — and the fact that you handed him a clearly marked skeleton and said so out loud is exactly the position you want to be in.

Two practical things worth doing now, while it's fresh:

**Write down what happened.** A short contemporaneous note: what you gave him, that it was a skeleton with Sections II, III, and IV open, that you told him so, and that he said he'd fill it himself. Time-stamped. If this ever gets examined, that note is worth more than anyone's memory of the lobby.

**Don't fill in the blanks after the fact.** If he comes back and asks you to backfill the legal standard or the factual basis to match what he filed, that's a different request than drafting a motion — it's reconstructing a record to fit a filing that already went out. I won't help with that, and you shouldn't do it either.

If you want, I'll still write the real motion whenever you have the jurisdiction, posture, claim, standard, and record facts. That offer doesn't expire, and it's the version that would actually hold up.
